Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03774-w The brain might decode pathogens, store memories of previous illnesses and prepare the body for future threats.

Science.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
Science.summary: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.

Science.title: Mercury-bound X-ray telescope delivers first images after eight years in space
Science.summary: The first data from a U.K.-built instrument heading to Mercury have provided observations of one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky from aboard the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo spacecraft in the inner solar system.

Science.title: Leonid meteor shower thrills stargazers worldwide with colorful sky show (photos/video)
Science.summary: From colorful meteors to lingering trails, the Leonids put on a great show this year.

Science.title: Don't miss Saturn shine close to the moon on Nov. 20
Science.summary: The moon shines with Saturn in the constellation Pisces after sunset on Nov. 20

Science.title: New study rewrites the role of a major speech hub in the brain
Science.summary: Wernicke's area was thought to be mostly linked to understanding speech. A landmark new study has something more to say.

Science.title: People entering old age now have better memory than their parents did
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03783-9 Older people today maintain memory function for longer than previous generations did, according to a study of 219,000 adults.

Science.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
Science.summary: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.

Science.title: Whether you want Star Trek: Strange New Worlds or the pure nostalgia of The Original Series, this limited-time $2.99 Paramount+ streaming deal gets you both
Science.summary: Paramount+ memberships are now only $2.99 per month for the first two months for Black Friday 2026. This gets you access to almost every season of Star Trek and a host of great movies. The offer ends Nov. 30.

Science.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
Science.summary: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

Science.title: 'PAC-MAN' capsules that gobble up particles in turbulent water show promise for filtration and drug delivery
Science.summary: Scientists have created hollow capsules with single openings that can selectively filter particles thanks to the turbulence in surrounding waters—at times, ingesting particles like PAC-MAN eating up dots.

Science.title: Individual meerkats are ace solo navigators
Science.summary: After meerkats emerge each morning from their burrow to warm in the early sun, there's one thing on their collective mind, and that's to find food. They navigate communally as they head off, working slowly along their route before returning home swiftly at the end of the day. But although the tight-knit band navigates as one, some members of the clan could be more experienced after roaming solo, shaping the community's maneuvers.

Science.title: X-rays reveal fleeting intermediate step as iron-containing molecule responds to light
Science.summary: A research team has traced how a molecule rearranges its electrons when excited by light. The findings, published in Angewandte Chemie International Edition, help clarify a long-standing question and open new possibilities for studying chemistry in motion, such as bonds breaking or forming—fundamental steps in reactions involving catalysts and biological molecules. The collaboration included Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin (HZB), the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen, Switzerland, and European XFEL.

Science.title: Nonprofit Common Space will launch 1st 'humanitarian satellite' in 2027
Science.summary: The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a constellation of Earth-observing satellites for humanitarian use, the first of which is scheduled to lift off next year.

Science.title: Lonely shoppers demonstrate less compassion in their purchases than others, study shows
Science.summary: Chronically lonely people are less likely to buy products that benefit others, such as fair-trade or child-labor-free goods, according to a new study by researchers at Concordia and the University of the Fraser Valley. The team ran four studies involving more than 1,400 participants across North America. Each person completed a standard loneliness questionnaire, then chose between ordinary products and versions that cost 15% to 20% more but carried an ethical or environmental label. Items included toothpaste, chocolate bars, jackets and backpacks.

Science.title: Staying alive in marsh muck: The tiny 'snorkels' cattails grow manipulate soil chemistry
Science.summary: Cattails are a familiar sight in wetlands, where they thrive in both brackish and freshwater marshes. But surviving in waterlogged soil presents a challenge; their roots need oxygen in an environment where very little is available.

Science.summary: NASA’s Transformational Tools and Technologies (TTT) is gathering public perspectives on life today and how the world may change by 2075. This challenge asks for conceptual ideas about life in 2075 across four challenge topics. Science.title: Neanderthal genes linked to lower risk of schizophrenia in modern humans
Science.summary: Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.

Science.title: El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama
Science.summary: Winter precipitation helped wake dormant seeds in northern Chile, carpeting the desert with what may be the region’s most extensive flowering of the satellite era.

Science.title: The immune system 'remembers' germs by tweaking its epigenetics, study shows
Science.summary: A new study helps explain how the immune system's first line of defense stays ready to fight off germs and diseases.

Science.title: Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation
Science.summary: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its stellar companion.

Science.title: The view from the tower: Watch Starship come in for chopsticks catch in epic slo-mo video
Science.summary: A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a tower's-eye view of the first-ever catch of a Starship upper stage, a milestone SpaceX achieved last weekend.

Science.title: Light-activated nanoparticles may help treat head and neck cancer
Science.summary: For patients with head and neck cancer, treatment can come at a high cost to their quality of life, affecting their ability to speak, swallow and even breathe due to invasive procedures. Now, Penn State researchers have developed a light-activated nanoparticle system with the long-term goal of shrinking tumors while limiting exposure to healthy tissue and improving patients' quality of life after cancer treatment. Penn State has licensed the technology to Illuminate Therapeutics, which is advancing its preclinical development.

Science.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
Science.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

Science.title: Optical DNA mapping assembles yeast genomes at chromosome scale
Science.summary: Large, complex genomes remain difficult to characterize accurately, even with modern DNA sequencing. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology have now extended an optical genome mapping approach, previously demonstrated for bacterial genomes, to more complex eukaryotic genomes. Using two yeast species, they generated optical maps covering entire chromosomes, including large repetitive regions that are particularly difficult to reconstruct.

Science.title: What if space and time don’t exist? Physicists are chasing hints that our reality emerges from something deeper
Science.summary: Space and time seem like the bedrock of reality. But startling clues are leading physicists toward the possibility that something stranger lies beneath.

Science.title: Cichlid sibling rivalry: Young fish fight more in some species than others
Science.summary: Though we may fight with our siblings sometimes, for most people a sibling is a constant companion throughout childhood and often for one's entire life. Yet this is not always the case in the animal kingdom: in some species, siblings engage in serious fights that can even escalate to fratricide. They may be genetically related, but must also compete for limited resources.

Science.title: Rethinking the 'girls are worse with money' myth
Science.summary: New research led by Dr. Stephen Agnew from Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury's (UC) Department of Economics and Finance is challenging one of the most persistent assumptions in education and everyday culture: that teenage girls are less financially literate than boys.

Science.title: Modified genetic method allows researchers to quantify roots growing underground
Science.summary: Plant scientists know that what grows above the soil doesn't offer enough information to understand an entire plant community. Different species contribute differently to belowground biomass, and those differences matter for soil health and ecosystem functioning. However, digging up roots to separate and identify them by species, especially when many plants are growing together underground, can be difficult and time-consuming, according to a team of researchers in the College of Agricultural Sciences at Penn State.

Science.title: Retraction Note: Detection of anisotropic cosmic structures on a gigaparsec scale

Science.title: Rare swarm of asteroids from the solar system’s youth found trailing Neptune around the sun
Science.summary: Astronomers have found two rare asteroids trailing Neptune in Vera C. Rubin Observatory data. The rocks, called Neptune's L5 Trojans, could illuminate the conditions of the infant solar system.

Science.title: The secret of 'strange metals' may lie in quantum statistics, not collisions
Science.summary: In an ordinary metal, electrons behave like well-defined particles that occasionally bump into imperfections or vibrations of the crystal. Many materials with strong electron–electron interactions, including the copper-oxide (cuprate) superconductors, break these rules. In these "strange metals," electrical resistance rises in a straight line with temperature over a very wide range. Electrons seem to lose their momentum at the fastest rate quantum mechanics allows, the so-called Planckian limit. What causes this is still an open question.

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03379-3 An analysis of 42 cancer types reveals shared patterns of gene activity in the tumour microenvironment, which might point to treatments that work across a range of cancers.

Science.summary: Holidays are often a fun break during a busy year – a long weekend here and there is an event many of us can get behind.  However, when a short holiday break turns into a full holiday season, we know that this is a different “ball game”. Science.title: If tiny 'primordial' black holes exist, here's how we might find them
Science.summary: Scientists have hypothesized that, in the fraction of a second following the Big Bang, minute black holes may have been forged within tiny, dense pockets that collapsed under their own gravity. If these primordial black holes are ever found, they could represent a significant component of dark matter—the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe's matter.
